49	
50	## Python environment
51	
52	Plugins that declare Python dependencies need a working Python environment. HCLI checks this before installing dependencies. If something is wrong, the install stops and points you to `hcli ida python doctor` for details. See [IDA's Python Environment](ida-python-environment.md) for setup.
53	
54	If your Python setup works but does not match the recommended configuration, pass `--no-python-environment-check` to skip the check:
55	
56	```console
57	❯ hcli plugin --no-python-environment-check install <name>
58	```
59	
60	## Plugin repositories
61	
62	HCLI fetches plugins from named repositories. Two are configured by default:
63	
64	| Name | Description | Authentication |
65	| :--- | :---------- | :------------- |
66	| `community` | Community plugins indexed from public GitHub repositories | none (anonymous) |
67	| `hexrays` | Private plugins published by Hex-Rays | required (`hcli login`) |
68	
69	The `community` repository is the default. A bare `hcli plugin install <name>` searches it. To install a private plugin from the `hexrays` repository, prefix the name:
70	
71	```console
72	❯ hcli plugin install hexrays/some-private-plugin
73	```
74	
75	If you're not logged in, the `hexrays` repository returns a 401 and HCLI tells you to authenticate. `hcli plugin search` spans all configured repositories and notes any it could not reach.
76	
77	### Managing repositories
78	
79	List, add, remove, or change the default repository:
80	
81	```console
82	❯ hcli plugin repo list
83	community  https://community.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json  default reserved
84	hexrays    https://hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json    reserved
85	
86	❯ hcli plugin repo add my-team https://plugins.example.com/repo.json
87	added plugin repository 'my-team' -> https://plugins.example.com/repo.json
88	
89	❯ hcli plugin repo set-default my-team
90	default plugin repository is now 'my-team'
91	
92	❯ hcli plugin repo remove my-team
93	removed plugin repository 'my-team'
94	```
95	
96	The `community` and `hexrays` names are reserved and always point to their Hex-Rays URLs. Custom repositories can be added, renamed, or removed freely.
97	
98	For offline or air-gapped environments like FLARE-VM, you can point HCLI at a local [plugin bundle](../reference/plugin-bundle-spec.md) instead of the online repositories. Pass `--repo` with a path to the bundle archive, and `search`, `install`, and `upgrade` all resolve from that local file without network access.
99	
100	```console
101	❯ hcli plugin --repo ./malware-vm-tools.hcli-plugin-bundle.zip search
102	❯ hcli plugin --repo ./malware-vm-tools.hcli-plugin-bundle.zip install hint-calls
103	```
104	
105	## As a user of IDA...
106	
107	You'll want to know the HCLI commands:
108	
109	```
110	❯ hcli plugin search 
111	❯ hcli plugin search [keyword or plugin-name]
112	❯ hcli plugin install <plugin-name>
113	❯ hcli plugin install <repo>/<plugin-name>
114	❯ hcli plugin status
115	❯ hcli plugin upgrade <plugin-name>
116	❯ hcli plugin uninstall <plugin-name>
117	❯ hcli plugin repo list
118	```
119	
120	Plugins are written to `$IDAUSR/plugins`, which is typically `~/.idapro/plugins` on Unix-like systems, where IDA Pro will load them the next time the application is opened.
121	
122	### Plugin dependencies
123	
124	A plugin can declare other plugins as dependencies in its `ida-plugin.json`. When you install or upgrade such a plugin, HCLI fetches the declared dependencies from the same repository and installs them as independent top-level plugins. If a dependency is already installed and satisfies the version requirement, it is skipped.
125	
126	On upgrade, HCLI installs any newly-added dependencies and tells you about any that were removed from the manifest (they stay installed so you can remove them yourself if no longer needed).
127	
128	On uninstall, HCLI lists installed dependencies and asks whether to remove them:
129	
130	```console
131	❯ hcli plugin uninstall my-suite
132	Uninstalled plugin: my-suite
133	These plugins were listed as dependencies:
134	  dep-a    1.0.0
135	  dep-b    2.3.0
136	Remove them too? [y/N]
137	```
138	
139	Pass `--yes` (`-y`) to confirm automatically in scripts. In non-interactive mode without `--yes`, dependencies are listed but not removed.
140	
141	You can discover interesting plugins via:
142	
143	  - `hcli plugin search` CLI program, or
144	  - [plugins.hex-rays.com](https://plugins.hex-rays.com) website, or
145	  - [github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository) raw index data on GitHub.
146	
147	HCLI supports installing plugins to be loaded by IDA 9.0 and newer.
148	
149	### Plugin repositories
150	
151	HCLI ships with two built-in repositories (`hexrays` and `community`) that provide the public plugin index. You can add your own named repositories that point to a JSON index file, a local directory of plugin archives, or a [plugin bundle](../reference/plugin-bundle-spec.md) zip.
152	
153	```
154	❯ hcli plugin repo list
155	❯ hcli plugin repo add <name> <url>
156	❯ hcli plugin repo remove <name>
157	❯ hcli plugin repo set-default <name>
158	```
159	
160	Repository URLs use the `https://` scheme for remote JSON indexes or `file://` for local paths. HCLI infers the repository type from what the path points to: a directory becomes a filesystem repository, a zip file containing `plugin-bundle.json` becomes a bundle repository, and anything else is treated as a JSON index.
161	
162	You can scope plugin references to a specific repository with a `repo/` prefix (e.g., `hcli plugin install myrepo/plugin-name`). Unprefixed references resolve against the default repository.
163	
164	### Offline and air-gapped environments
165	
166	Environments without internet access (for example, a FLARE-VM instance with host-only networking) can use a plugin bundle as their sole repository. A plugin bundle is a self-contained zip archive with plugins and their Python dependencies for specific platforms. See [Plugin Bundles](../reference/plugin-bundle-spec.md) for the format.
167	
168	To set this up, remove the default repositories (which require network access), add the bundle as a named repository, and set it as the default:
169	
170	```console
171	❯ hcli plugin repo remove hexrays
172	removed plugin repository 'hexrays'
173	
174	❯ hcli plugin repo remove community
175	removed plugin repository 'community'
176	
177	❯ hcli plugin repo add offline file:///path/to/plugin-bundle.zip
178	added plugin repository 'offline' -> file:///path/to/plugin-bundle.zip
179	
180	❯ hcli plugin repo set-default offline
181	default plugin repository is now 'offline'
182	
183	❯ hcli plugin search
184	current platform: windows-x86_64
185	current version: 9.4
186	
187	 plugin1  1.0.0  ...
188	
189	❯ hcli plugin install plugin1
190	Installed plugin: plugin1==1.0.0
191	```
192	
193	Dependencies are installed from the bundle's embedded wheelhouse, so pip does not need network access.
194	
195	To restore the default configuration later, re-add the built-in repositories with their canonical URLs:
196	
197	```console
198	❯ hcli plugin repo add hexrays https://hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json
199	❯ hcli plugin repo add community https://community.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json
200	```
201	
202	### Disambiguating plugin names
203	
204	When two plugins share the same bare name in the repository (for example, different forks of the same project), HCLI cannot tell which one you mean from the name alone. The `search`, `install`, and `upgrade` commands will print the ambiguous candidates and ask you to qualify the reference with the plugin's repository URL:
205	
206	```console
207	❯ hcli plugin install ida-chat
208	Error: plugin name 'ida-chat' is ambiguous
209	Choose one of:
210	  ida-chat@https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-chat-plugin
211	  ida-chat@https://github.com/tanu360/ida-chat-plugin
212	```
213	
214	You can pin the reference with `name@repository-url`, and optionally include a version spec:
215	
216	```console
217	❯ hcli plugin install ida-chat@https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-chat-plugin
218	❯ hcli plugin install ida-chat==1.0.0@https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-chat-plugin
219	```
220	
221	Because plugins install into `$IDAUSR/plugins/<name>`, only one plugin with a given bare name can be installed at a time. If you need to switch to a different same-named plugin from another repository, uninstall the current one first. Similarly, `upgrade` will not change the source repository: once a plugin is installed, its repository is recorded in the local metadata and upgrades are anchored to it.
222

1	# IDA Plugin Repository Architecture
2	
3	## Core Components
4	
5	The plugin system has several components:
6	
7	[plugins.hex-rays.com](https://plugins.hex-rays.com/) is a web interface showing the available IDA plugins.
8	
9	A **GitHub indexer** ([github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository)) runs regularly, discovers plugins across public GitHub repositories, and publishes a JSON index. The raw index data is available [on GitHub](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/refs/heads/v1/plugin-repository.json).
10	
11	The **community repository** at `community.plugins.hex-rays.com` mirrors this GitHub index. HCLI fetches from this URL by default. The **hexrays repository** at `hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com` serves private plugins published by Hex-Rays, available to users with active IDA licenses. It requires authentication via `hcli login`.
12	
13	HCLI reads its repositories from `.Settings.plugin-repositories` in `ida-config.json` and merges them client-side, so it always knows which repository served a plugin. Two are shipped and reserved: `community` (anonymous) and `hexrays` (authenticated). Additional repositories can be managed with `hcli plugin repo list | add | remove | set-default`. See [Plugin Manager](../user-guide/plugin-manager.md#plugin-repositories) for usage.
14	
15	A reference may name a repository: `hcli plugin install hexrays/<name>`. Without a prefix, it resolves in the default repository (`community`). `hcli plugin search` spans every configured repository and reports any it could not reach.
16	
17	
18	## How It Works
19	
20	The plugin repository's GitHub Action watches for GitHub repositories that contain an `ida-plugin.json` file.
21	For each repo, it will watch for releases. When it sees a release, it will inspect the release archives for either source archives (pure-Python) or binary archives (containing .so/.dll/.dylib plugins).
22	In either case, it'll expect to find an `ida-plugin.json` file in the archive describing the plugin.
23	The service will index all the found archives and their metadata, and expose this to HCLI
24	(and/or other plugin managers, like a planned GUI version within IDA).
25	
26	!!! note
27	
28	    The plugin repository requires additional metadata compared to the initial version documented on the Hex-Rays docs website.
29	
30	
31	## IDA Plugin Manager
32	
33	HCLI fetches the plugin repository JSON from each configured repository to list/search for plugins and retrieve download URLs.
34	After various validation steps, HCLI then extracts the archive subdirectory containing
35	 `ida-plugin.json` into `$IDAUSR/plugins/`, and the plugin is installed.
36	If there are Python dependencies declared within the metadata file, then these are installed via pip first.
37	There are obvious upgrade and uninstallation routines, too.
38	
39	### Plugin Installation Location
40	
41	Plugins are installed to `$IDAUSR/plugins/`, where `$IDAUSR` is the IDA user directory: 
42	
43	- **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\Hex-Rays\IDA Pro\`
44	- **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/IDA Pro/`
45	- **Linux**: `~/.idapro/`
46	
47	It's possible to override `$IDAUSR` when running IDA, which can be helpful if you test across multiple versions:
48	
49	```
50	$ export IDAUSR=~/.idapro91/
51	$ hcli plugin install ipyida
52	$ ~/software/ida-9.1/ida
53	```
54	
55	Each plugin is installed in its own subdirectory within `plugins/`. For example, installing the "oplog" plugin creates:
56	```
57	$IDAUSR/plugins/oplog/
58	├── ida-plugin.json
59	├── oplog_entry.py
60	└── (other plugin files)
61	```
62	
63	The directory name matches the plugin name from `ida-plugin.json`.
64	This is why the contents of `name` are fairly restrictive. They should also be globally unique.
65	
66	During upgrades, the existing directory is replaced with the new version.
67	Uninstallation is as easy as deleting the directory.
68	
69	### Plugin identity and name collisions
70	
71	In the repository index, a plugin is identified by the pair `(name, repository URL)`. Two plugins with the same bare name from different repositories are distinct entries, and the repository URL is normalized (lowercased scheme/host/path, trailing slash stripped) before comparison so that cosmetic URL differences do not split a single plugin into two.
72	
73	On disk, however, plugins still install as `$IDAUSR/plugins/<name>`. Name is therefore the installed-layout identity, and only one plugin with a given bare name can be installed at a time. When the repository contains multiple plugins with the same name, HCLI requires a qualified reference of the form `name@repository-url` (optionally with a version spec, e.g. `name==1.2.3@repository-url`). An installed plugin's local metadata records its source repository, so status and upgrade operations anchor their repository lookups on the installed plugin's host and stay consistent even when the bare name is ambiguous in the repository.
74

1	# Publishing your plugin to the IDA Plugin Repository
2	
3	## Why Publish Your Plugin?
4	
5	As the author of an existing or new plugin, we encourage you to make the following updates so that your project is compatible with the HCLI and Plugin Manager, and can benefit from the new ecosystem. 
6	
7	Making your plugin available via Plugin Manager offers several benefits:
8	
9	  - simplified plugin installation
10	  - improved plugin discoverability through the central index
11	  - easy Python dependency management
12	
13	
14	If you have any questions, open an issue on [this repo](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli) or contact our [support](https://support.hex-rays.com/).
15	
16	
17	!!! note "Coming Soon"
18	
19	      We plan to add plugin configuration management to handle things like user preferences, API key storage, etc.
20	
21	
22	If you're having trouble or don't have the bandwidth, please don't hesitate to reach out to us at Hex-Rays - we're here to support you.
23	
24	## Steps to Publication
25	
26	The key points to make your IDA plugin available via Plugin Manager are:
27	
28	  1. Update `ida-plugin.json`
29	  2. Package your plugin into a ZIP archive
30	  3. Publish releases on GitHub
31	
32	For further details on how your plugin fits into the greater ecosystem, you can also review:
33	
34	  - [Plugin packaging and format](./plugin-packaging-and-format.md)
35	  - [Plugin repository architecture](./plugin-repository-architecture.md)
36	
37	
38	The community plugin ecosystem is fully automated. After you publish a new GitHub release with updated metadata, your plugin is automatically indexed and served through the `community` plugin repository.
39	
40	
41	### 1. Update or create `ida-plugin.json`
42	
43	IDA 9.0 introduced `ida-plugin.json` as a way to [declare metadata about plugins](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing), such as name and entry point.
44	We extend this format with **new required and optional fields** to ensure compatibility with HCLI and the Plugin Manager, and to make the metadata more informative.
45	
46	A minimal `ida-plugin.json` file now looks like:
47	
48	```json
49	{
50	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
51	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
52	  "plugin": {
53	    "name": "plugin1",
54	    "version": "1.0.0",
55	    "entryPoint": "plugin1.py",
56	    "urls": {
57	      "repository": "https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli"
58	    },
59	    "authors": [{
60	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
61	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
62	    }]
63	  }
64	}
65	```
66	
67	and a more complete `ida-plugin.json` looks like:
68	
69	```json
70	{
71	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
72	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
73	  "plugin": {
74	    "name": "ida-terminal-plugin",
75	    "entryPoint": "index.py",
76	    "version": "1.0.0",
77	    "idaVersions": [
78	      "9.0",
79	      "9.1",
80	      "9.2"
81	    ],
82	    "platforms": [
83	      "windows-x86_64",
84	      "linux-x86_64",
85	      "macos-x86_64",
86	      "macos-aarch64",
87	    ],
88	    "description": "A lightweight terminal integration for IDA Pro that lets you open a fully functional terminal within the IDA GUI.\nQuickly access shell commands, scripts, or tooling without leaving your reversing environment.",
89	    "license": "MIT",
90	    "logoPath": "ida-plugin.png",
91	    "categories": [
92	      "ui-ux-and-visualization"
93	    ],
94	    "keywords": [
95	      "terminal",
96	      "shell",
97	      "cli",
98	    ],
99	    "pythonDependencies": [
100	      "pydantic>=2.12"
101	    ],
102	    "urls": {
103	      "repository": "https://github.com/williballenthin/idawilli"
104	    },
105	    "authors": [{
106	      "name": "Pierre-Alexandre Losson",
107	      "email": "palosson@hex-rays.com"
108	    }],
109	    "maintainers": [{
110	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
111	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
112	    }],
113	    "settings": [
114	      {
115	        "key": "theme",
116	        "type": "string",
117	        "required": true,
118	        "default": "darcula",
119	        "name": "color theme",
120	        "documentation": "the color theme name, picked from https://windowsterminalthemes.dev/",
121	      }
122	    ]
123	  }
124	}
125	```
126	
127	Here are the **new required** fields:
128	
129	  - `.plugin.version` is now required
130	  - `.plugin.urls.repository` is required
131	  - `.plugin.authors` and/or `.plugin.maintainers` must be provided, `.email` is required
132	
133	and new optional fields:
134	
135	  - `.plugin.pythonDependencies` is a list of packages on PyPI that will be installed
136	  - `.plugin.keywords` is a list of terms to help users searching for plugins
137	  - `.plugin.platforms` is recommended, defaults to all platforms. The possible values are: `windows-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64`, `macos-x86_64`, and `macos-aarch64`.
138	  - `.plugin.license` for the code license of your project
139	  - `.plugin.settings` is a list of descriptors of settings
140	  - `.plugin.dependencies` declares companion plugins to install alongside this one (e.g., `["dep-a", "dep-b==1.0.0"]`)
141	
142	
143	!!! tip "Validating Your `ida-plugin.json` File"
144	
145	    If there's a problem with the `ida-plugin.json` file, then it will not be indexed by the plugin repository. Unfortunately even things like trailing commas will break strict JSON parsers like the one used by HCLI.  
146	    We recommend to use `hcli plugin lint /path/to/plugin[.zip]` to check for problems and suggestions.
147	
148	
149	### 2. Package your plugin
150	
151	You must distribute plugins via ZIP archives.
152	See [Plugin packaging and format](./plugin-packaging-and-format.md) for more details on the contents of the ZIP archives.
153	Essentially, collect the plugin files (Python source or `.dll`/`.so`/`.dylib` shared objects) and the `ida-plugin.json` and any other supporting resources into a single file.
154	
155	- For **pure-Python plugins**, you can probably rely on the source archive automatically attached to GitHub Releases and Tags.
156	- For **native plugins**, you should consider using GitHub Actions to build the artifacts - and Hex-Rays is happy to provide templates and/or propose an initial workflow. You can see an example here: [milankovo/zydisinfo .../build.yml](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/blob/main/.github/workflows/build.yml)
157	
158	#### Packaging Pure Python Plugins
159	
160	For simple single-file plugins, all you need to do is add an `ida-plugin.json` file.
161	Then do releases via GitHub Actions and the automatically attached source archive will be the plugin archive.
162	
163	In fact, most pure Python plugins can get away with no build step, and just tagging releases via GitHub Releases.
164	
165	If there are multiple plugins in the same repo, this is ok, as long as they're in separate directories.
166	See "Multi-Plugin Archives" in [Plugin packaging and format](./plugin-packaging-and-format.md).
167	
168	If a Python plugin relies on a third-party dependency, declare this in the `pythonDependencies` array in `ida-plugin.json`.
169	
170	If there's many files related to the plugin, ensure they're all in the same directory (or nested subdirectory) as `ida-plugin.json`.
171	Python plugins can rely on imports relative to the entry point script, so the following are ok:
172	
173	```
174	plugins.zip
175	└── plugin1
176	    ├── ida-plugin.json
177	    ├── plugin_entry.py
178	    └── myutils.py
179	
180	# import myutils
181	```
182	
183	or
184	
185	```
186	plugins.zip
187	└── plugin1
188	    ├── ida-plugin.json
189	    ├── plugin_entry.py
190	    └── mylib
191	        ├── __init__.py
192	        └── foo
193	
194	# import mylib.foo
195	```
196	
197	Some plugins have published most of their code to PyPI via a traditional Python package, and then refer to this in a trivial entrypoint stub.
198	This is fine. IPyIDA is an example.
199	They can keep doing this, updating `pythonDependencies` to reference that package; or they can package the Python code as a relative import.
200	
201	
202	#### Packaging a Native Plugin
203	
204	If its a native plugin, adapt the build configuration (if it exists) to GitHub Actions.
205	To acquire the SDK, either use a Git submodule or use HCLI to fetch it.
206	The latter is probably a better solution but requires an active IDA Pro license (but you can get one through the [Plugin Contributor Program](https://hex-rays.com/contributor-program)),
207	and enables you to build against 8.4, 9.0, 9.1, as well as 9.2+.
208	The open source SDK on GitHub only has tags for 9.2+.
209	
210	Here's an example workflow: [PR#4](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/pull/4)
211	
212	Once you have built the shared object files, package them up along with the `ida-plugin.json` file.
213	You can create one artifact per platform, or do a "fat" binary archive (see above).
214	Separate files might be easier; just make sure you set `.plugin.platforms` in `ida-plugin.json` to reflect the contents, so we don't try to install .dll files on macOS.
215	
216	#### Example: Packaging eset/DelphiHelper
217	
218	Because this is a pure-Python plugin, packaging was very easy! Just add the metadata file and do releases on GitHub:
219	
220	1. added `ida-plugin.json`: [PR#5](https://github.com/eset/DelphiHelper/pull/5/files)
221	2. asked to start using GitHub Releases via the web interface
222	3. ...done
223	
224	
225	#### Example: Packaging milankovo/zydishelper
226	
227	Because this is a plugin written in C++ and compiled to a native shared object, packaging took a little more work:
228	
229	1. added `ida-plugin.json`: [PR#4](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/pull/4/files#diff-601834cd7516c6a40f96dda33295f21abd1f8e96f85095ab0823375f6479da3f)
230	2. added a [workflow for GitHub Actions](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/pull/4/files#diff-5c3fa597431eda03ac3339ae6bf7f05e1a50d6fc7333679ec38e21b337cb6721) to build the plugin
231	  a. use [HCLI](https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/) to fetch IDA Pro SDKs for 9.0, 9.1, and 9.2
232	  b. use [ida-cmake](https://github.com/allthingsida/ida-cmake) for configuration
233	  c. matrixed across Windows/Linux/macOS runners
234	  d. build the plugin
235	  e. upload to the GitHub Releases page
236	3. asked to start using [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/releases) via the web interface
237	
238	While it took a little while to get working, this workflow should serve as a solid template for many plugins written in C++.
239	For example, we used it to kickstart the [build of the BinDiff plugin](https://github.com/HexRays-plugin-contributions/bindiff/blob/ci-gha/.github/workflows/build.yml).
240	
241	### 3. Publish releases on GitHub
242	
243	The community plugin index is built from GitHub. Publish releases on GitHub with valid `ida-plugin.json` files and the indexer will pick them up automatically.
244	
245	Upload plugin archives as attachments to the release (unless the default source archive is sufficient, which is usually true for pure-Python plugins). Each day, the indexer scans GitHub for repositories containing `ida-plugin.json` and inspects their releases for candidate plugins. The indexed results are served through the `community` plugin repository.
246	
247	Inclusion into the community repository is self-service: put a well-formed plugin in a place the indexer can find it.
248	
249	!!! tip "Test your plugin"
250	
251	      Check out [our guide](../how-to/test-plugin-before-publishing.md) to test your plugin before publishing it to the new Plugin Manager ecosystem.
252	
253	
254	## FAQ
255	
256	### Do I need to submit my plugin anywhere?
257	
258	No. If you publish GitHub Releases with valid `ida-plugin.json` files, your plugin is automatically indexed into the `community` repository. The flow is self-service and open.
259	
260	### What do I do if my plugin doesn't show up in the repo?
261	
262	1. Ensure the plugin file (the ZIP archive) is well formed: `hcli plugin lint /path/to/plugin.zip`
263	2. Check that plugin is recognized by the indexer by inspecting [plugin-repository.json](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/blob/v1/plugin-repository.json).
264	    1. ensure you can find your plugin in the [search results](https://github.com/search?q=path%3A**%2Fida-plugin.json&type=code)
265	    2. otherwise, you can propose to add your plugin to the explicit list here: [known-repositories.json](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/blob/v1/known-repositories.txt)
266	3. Open an issue [here](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/issues) and Hex-Rays will be happy to help debug
267	
268	
269	The indexer runs daily, so it might take a little time for your plugin to show up.
270	Feel free to ping us and we can manually trigger a rebuild to check for your new plugin.
271	
272	
273	### How can I report a suspicious/malicious plugin?
274	
275	Open an issue on the plugin repository and the Hex-Rays team will investigate and potentially update the index.
276	
277	
278	### How does moderation work?
279	
280	Plugins can be removed from the plugin repository so that HCLI does not serve them to users.
281	
282	At a technical level, the plugin repository *is* the JSON file available [here](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository).
283	Its produced by an indexer that runs periodically, and uses a [denylist](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/blob/v1/ignored-repositories.txt) to filter out repositories that Hex-Rays deems inappropriate (malware, illegal, abusive, etc.).
284	Because the entire repository is within a git repository on GitHub, anyone can review the enforcement actions (such as adding to the denylist) and see what has happened.
285	We designed transparency into the system from the start, to help everyone understand and trust the infrastructure.
286	
287	### I previously submitted my plugin via My Hex-Rays portal. What should I do now?
288	
289	Follow the guidelines on [making your plugin compatible with Plugin Manager](../reference/packaging-your-existing-plugin.md). Once completed, your plugin will be included in the central index and available directly through the Plugin Manager.
290	
291	If your plugin is hosted in the same repository used for your previous submission to [plugins.hex-rays.com](https://plugins.hex-rays.com/), and the repository URL remains unchanged, we’ll automatically update its details on the website.
292	
293	
294	
295	
296

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   The user asked me to read a design document (`~/Obsidian/hex-rays/hcli/plugin components and dependencies design.md`) and implement "tightly coupled plugin suites" via a `components` field on `PluginMetadata`. The loose `dependencies` field was already implemented. After thorough research and presenting an implementation plan, the user approved and asked me to implement, commit incrementally, push, open a PR, and babysit CI. Subsequently, the user asked me to review existing documentation and suggest/make updates for the new feature.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - `components` field: `list[str]` on `PluginMetadata` for declaring tightly-coupled plugin suites. Components are subdirectories bundled inside the suite's archive, share the suite's lifecycle, hidden from top-level listings.
   - `dependencies` field: Already implemented loose coupling where plugins are fetched individually and installed as independent top-level plugins.
   - Component tree walking: Recursive traversal from directories and archives, depth-limited to 10 (matching IDA's `enumerate_fs_recursive`).
   - Root manifest identification: In multi-manifest archives, the root is the manifest not referenced as a component by any other manifest.
   - Name collision checking: Component names checked against all installed top-level plugins and other suites' components.
   - `get_installed_plugin_records()` is one-level-deep — components in nested dirs are naturally hidden.
   - `extract_zip_subdirectory_to()` extracts full subtrees — component subdirectories come for free.
   - Trash-and-replace upgrade mechanism handles suite upgrades atomically.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`src/hcli/lib/ida/plugin/__init__.py`** (worktree)
     - Added `components: list[str]` field to `PluginMetadata` with `@field_validator` rejecting version pins (`==`), host qualifiers (`@`), invalid names, and duplicates.
     - JSON schema auto-updates from Pydantic.

   - **`src/hcli/lib/ida/plugin/components.py`** (NEW, worktree)
     - Core utilities: `walk_component_tree_from_directory()`, `walk_component_tree_from_archive()`, `find_root_manifest_in_archive()`, `find_suite_for_component()`, `check_component_name_collisions()`, `collect_all_component_names_from_archive()`, `collect_python_dependencies_from_component_tree()`
     - Uses `TYPE_CHECKING` guard for `InstalledPluginRecord` to avoid circular imports.

   - **`src/hcli/commands/plugin/install.py`** (worktree)
     - 5 `len(items) != 1` checks relaxed to allow suite archives: if 0 items reject, if 1 item use directly, if >1 use `find_root_manifest_in_archive`.
     - Added collision checking before install: `find_suite_for_component()` refuses if name is a component of existing suite; `check_component_name_collisions()` checks all component names.

   - **`src/hcli/commands/plugin/uninstall.py`** (worktree)
     - Component uninstall refused via `find_suite_for_component()` check before `uninstall_plugin_impl`.
     - Suite uninstall lists managed components with versions, prompts "Uninstall all? [Y/n]" (default yes, auto with --yes/non-interactive).

   - **`src/hcli/commands/plugin/status.py`** (worktree)
     - Added `ComponentInfo` model (name, version) and `components: list[ComponentInfo] | None` to `InstalledPluginStatusEntry`.
     - `_collect_components()` walks component tree for each record.
     - Text output shows "(N components)" on suite entries.
     - `--show-components` flag expands suites to show indented component rows.
     - JSON output naturally includes `components` array.

   - **`src/hcli/commands/plugin/lint.py`** (worktree)
     - Added `_check_components_in_directory()` and `_check_components_in_archive()` functions.
     - Validates component references, checks name matches, detects duplicates, recursively lints component metadata.

   - **`tests/lib/test_plugin_components.py`** (NEW, worktree)
     - 32 tests covering: metadata field validation, root manifest identification, archive tree walking, suite install/upgrade/uninstall, status display (count, --show-components, JSON), collision checking, find_suite_for_component, lint validation.
     - Helpers: `_make_suite_zip()`, `_make_nested_suite_zip()`, `_make_standalone_zip()`.

   - **`tests/lib/test_plugin_collisions.py`** (worktree)
     - Fixed `test_status_json_installed_plugin` to include `"components": None` in expected JSON output.

   - **`docs/schemas/ida-plugin.json`** (worktree)
     - Regenerated via `uv run hcli plugin schema -o docs/schemas/ida-plugin.json`.

   - **`~/Obsidian/hex-rays/hcli/plugin components implementation plan.md`** (written)
     - 12-step implementation plan with backlink to design doc.

4. Errors and fixes:
   - **ModuleNotFoundError for `hcli.lib.ida.plugin.components`**: Tests couldn't find the new module because `uv sync --extra test` hadn't been run in the worktree. Fixed by running `uv sync --extra test`.
   - **Circular import with `InstalledPluginRecord`**: `components.py` imported from `install.py` which imports from `__init__.py`. Fixed by using `TYPE_CHECKING` guard and lazy imports in function bodies.

1	## Plugin Packaging and Format
2	
3	A Plugin Archive is a ZIP archive that contains an IDA plugin and its associated `ida-plugin.json` metadata file.
4	The metadata file should be found in the root directory of the plugin within the archive.
5	
6	For example:
7	
8	```
9	plugin.zip
10	├── ida-plugin.json
11	└── plugin.py
12	```
13	
14	Or for a native plugin:
15	
16	```
17	plugin.zip
18	├── ida-plugin.json
19	├── plugin.so
20	├── plugin.dylib
21	└── plugin.dll
22	```
23	
24	### ida-plugin.json
25	
26	The [`ida-plugin.json` file](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing) is the marker for an IDA Pro plugin.
27	A typical `ida-plugin.json` file might look like this:
28	
29	```json
30	{
31	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
32	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
33	  "plugin": {
34	    "name": "oplog",
35	    "entryPoint": "oplog_entry.py",
36	    "version": "0.1.2",
37	    "idaVersions": ["9.1", "9.2"],
38	    "description": "oplog is an IDA Pro plugin that records operations during analysis.",
39	    "license": "Apache 2.0",
40	    "categories": [
41	      "ui-ux-and-visualization"
42	    ],
43	    "pythonDependencies": ["pydantic>=2"],
44	    "urls": {
45	      "repository": "https://github.com/williballenthin/idawilli"
46	    },
47	    "authors": [{
48	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
49	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
50	    }],
51	    "keywords": [
52	      "activity-tracking",
53	      "workflow-analysis",
54	      "reverse-engineering-methodology",
55	      "ai-training-data",
56	      "analysis-visualization"
57	    ]
58	  }
59	}
60	```
61	
62	And a minimal `ida-plugin.json` could look like this:
63	
64	```json
65	{
66	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
67	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
68	  "plugin": {
69	    "name": "oplog",
70	    "entryPoint": "oplog_entry.py",
71	    "version": "0.1.2",
72	    "urls": {
73	      "repository": "https://github.com/williballenthin/idawilli"
74	    },
75	    "authors": [{
76	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
77	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
78	    }]
79	  }
80	}
81	```
82	
83	In addition to the primary fields described initially on the [Hex-Rays docs](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing), **HCLI compatibility added new, required fields** in `ida-plugin.json`:
84	
85	  - `version`: the version of the plugin archive
86	  - `urls.repository`: the repository that publishes the plugin
87	  - `authors` (or `maintainers`): name and/or email. Social media handles are ok!
88	
89	And there are new optional fields:
90	
91	  - `.plugin.pythonDependencies` is a list of packages on PyPI that will be installed
92	  - `.plugin.keywords` is a list of terms to help users searching for plugins
93	  - `.plugin.platforms` is recommended, defaults to all platforms. The possible values are: `windows-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64`, `macos-x86_64`, and `macos-aarch64`.
94	  - `.plugin.license` for the code license of your project
95	  - `.plugin.settings` is a list of descriptors of settings
96	  - `.plugin.dependencies` declares companion plugins to install alongside this one (e.g., `["dep-a", "dep-b==1.0.0"]`)
97	
98	If there's a problem with the `ida-plugin.json` file, then the plugin is invalid and won't work with the repo.
99	Unfortunately even things like trailing commas will break strict JSON parsers like the one used by HCLI.
100	So, you can use `hcli plugin lint /path/to/plugin[.zip]` to check for problems and suggestions.
101	
102	!!! tip "Editor validation with JSON Schema"
103	
104	    HCLI publishes a JSON Schema for `ida-plugin.json` at
105	    [`https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json`](https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json).
106	
107	    Reference it from the top of your `ida-plugin.json` to get inline validation,
108	    autocompletion, and hover documentation in editors like VSCode:
109	
110	    ```json
111	    {
112	      "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
113	      "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
114	      "plugin": { ... }
115	    }
116	    ```
117	
118	    The schema is generated from the same Pydantic models HCLI uses to validate
119	    plugins, so editor warnings match what `hcli plugin lint` will report.
120	
121	
122	### Shared Settings
123	
124	HCLI is aware of settings that plugins declare in `ida-plugin.json` and prompts users for their value
125	during installation. The settings are written into `ida-config.json` and can be queried at plugin runtime
126	using the [ida-settings](https://pypi.org/project/ida-settings/) (v3) Python package:
127	
128	```py
129	import ida_settings
130	
131	api_key = ida_settings.get_current_plugin_setting("openai_key")
132	```
133	
134	Plugin authors are encouraged to adopt this configuration system, as it provides a centralized way to manage edits from both the CLI and (eventually) the GUI, users don't have to manually edit source code/config files,
135	and the data can be easily exported/imported.
136	
137	!!! note "Coming Soon"
138	
139	      The associated IDA plugin `ida-settings-editor` that lets users configure plugin settings within IDA is not yet available. We plan to introduce it in a future release.
140	
141	#### Setting Fields
142	
143	Each setting in the `settings` array supports the following fields:
144	
145	| Field | Type | Required | Description |
146	|-------|------|----------|-------------|
147	| `key` | string | yes | Unique code-level identifier (e.g., `"api_key"`) |
148	| `type` | string | yes | Either `"string"` or `"boolean"` |
149	| `required` | boolean | yes | Whether the setting must be provided |
150	| `default` | string/boolean | no | Default value when not configured |
151	| `name` | string | yes | Human-readable name (e.g., `"OpenAI API key"`) |
152	| `documentation` | string | no | Human-readable explanation |
153	| `validation_pattern` | string | no | Regex pattern for string validation |
154	| `choices` | array | no | List of acceptable string values |
155	| `prompt` | boolean | no | Whether to prompt during installation (default: `true`) |
156	
157	Setting `"prompt": false` is useful for advanced or niche settings that have sensible defaults and shouldn't clutter the installation experience. These settings can still be configured later via `hcli plugin config`.
158	
159	Example settings configuration:
160	
161	```json
162	{
163	  "settings": [
164	    {
165	      "key": "api_key",
166	      "type": "string",
167	      "required": true,
168	      "name": "API Key",
169	      "documentation": "Your API key from https://example.com/keys"
170	    },
171	    {
172	      "key": "cache_size",
173	      "type": "string",
174	      "required": false,
175	      "default": "100",
176	      "name": "Cache Size",
177	      "documentation": "Maximum number of cached items",
178	      "prompt": false
179	    }
180	  ]
181	}
182	```
183	
184	
185	### Plugin Dependencies
186	
187	A plugin can declare other plugins as loose dependencies via the `dependencies` field. Each entry is a plugin reference: a bare name, a name with a version pin, or a name with a repository host URL and optional version pin.
188	
189	```json
190	{
191	  "plugin": {
192	    "dependencies": [
193	      "go-runtime-detector",
194	      "go-string-extractor==1.2.0",
195	      "helper@https://github.com/org/repo"
196	    ]
197	  }
198	}
199	```
200	
201	When a user installs or upgrades a plugin that declares dependencies, HCLI fetches each one from the same repository and installs it as an independent top-level plugin. Dependencies that are already installed and satisfy the spec are skipped. If a pinned dependency is installed at a lower version, it is upgraded automatically; a higher installed version is not downgraded.
202	
203	Dependencies are not bundled inside the declaring plugin's archive. Each dependency is its own plugin with its own `ida-plugin.json` and its own archive in the repository.
204	
205	### Source Archives and Binary Archives
206	
207	For many pure-Python IDA plugins, source archives are often sufficient.
208	This means you don't have to create any GitHub Actions workflows; you just have to tag your releases in GitHub.
209	
210	If you distribute your pure-Python IDA plugin via PyPI, [like IPyIDA does](https://github.com/eset/ipyida),
211	then the plugin directory in your source archive becomes very simple.
212	You can put the following content in a subdirectory of the project (preferred), or publish a separate repository for the metadata:
213	
214	
215	```
216	.
217	├── ida-plugin.json
218	└── entry_stub.py
219	```
220	
221	With `ida-plugin.json`:
222	
223	```json
224	{
225	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
226	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
227	  "plugin": {
228	    "name": "plugin1",
229	    "entryPoint": "entry_stub.py",
230	    "version": "1.0",
231	    "idaVersions": ["9.0", "9.1", "9.2"],
232	    "pythonDependencies": ["ida-plugin1==1.0"],
233	    "urls": {
234	      "repository": "https://github.com/foo/bar"
235	    },
236	    "authors": [{
237	      "email": "user@example.com"
238	    }]
239	  }
240	}
241	```
242	
243	And the entry stub:
244	
245	
246	```py
247	from ida_plugin1.ida_plugin import PLUGIN_ENTRY
248	```
249	
250	### "Fat" Binary Plugin Archives
251	
252	Plugin archives can contain multiple compiled versions of a plugin, e.g., `foo-plugin.so` and `foo-plugin.dylib`.
253	In this case, the entry point must specify the bare path to the plugin, e.g., `foo-plugin`, and IDA will append the appropriate extension based on the platform.
254	You don't have to support all platforms. It's acceptable to publish multiple "thin" archives, one for each platform; however, "fat" archives are convenient.
255	
256	The file extensions must be exactly:
257	
258	  - `.dll` - Windows x86-64
259	  - `.so` - Linux 86-64
260	  - `_x86_64.dylib` - macOS x86_64 (not yet supported by IDA)
261	  - `_aarch64.dylib` - macOS aarch64 (not yet supported by IDA)
262	  - `.dylib` - macOS Universal Binary, only if Intel/ARM dylibs aren't present. (note: you must use this for macOS currently)
263	
264	
265	
266	Remember, plugin names must be unique within a plugin archive, which means:
267	
268	Allowed:
269	```
270	root/
271	  plugin/
272	    ida-plugin.json (name: foo-plugin)
273	    foo-plugin.so
274	    foo-plugin.dylib
275	    foo-plugin.dll
276	```
277	
278	Disallowed:
279	```
280	root/
281	  plugin-linux/
282	    ida-plugin.json (name: foo-plugin)
283	    foo-plugin.so
284	  plugin-windows/
285	    ida-plugin.json (name: foo-plugin)  <-- name collides!
286	    foo-plugin.dll
287	```
288	
289	### (uncommon) Multi-Plugin Archives
290	
291	Because the `ida-plugin.json` file marks the root of a plugin within the archive, an archive can contain multiple plugins:
292	
293	```
294	plugins.zip
295	├── plugin1
296	│   ├── plugin1.py
297	│   └── ida-plugin.json
298	└── plugin2
299	    ├── plugin2.py
300	    └── ida-plugin.json
301	```
302	
303	Plugin archives can also be collected into a [plugin bundle](./plugin-bundle-spec.md) for offline installation on air-gapped machines.
304

Dependencies are not bundled inside the declaring plugin's archive. Each dependency is its own plugin with its own `ida-plugin.json` and its own archive in the repository.

### Plugin Suites (Components)

When several plugins are tightly coupled and must be installed, upgraded, and removed as a unit, a plugin can declare them as **components** via the `components` field. Unlike loose dependencies, components are bundled inside the same archive as the declaring plugin (the "suite root") and share its lifecycle.

```json
{
  "plugin": {
    "name": "go-analysis-suite",
    "version": "2.0.0",
    "entryPoint": "go_suite.py",
    "components": ["go-runtime-detector", "go-string-extractor"],
    "urls": { "repository": "https://github.com/example/go-suite" },
    "authors": [{ "name": "Jane Doe" }]
  }
}
```

Each component is a subdirectory that contains its own `ida-plugin.json`. The directory name must match the component's `plugin.name`. Components can themselves declare further components, up to a nesting depth of 10.

```
go-analysis-suite.zip
└── go-analysis-suite/
    ├── ida-plugin.json          (name: go-analysis-suite, components: [...])
    ├── go_suite.py
    ├── go-runtime-detector/
    │   ├── ida-plugin.json      (name: go-runtime-detector)
    │   └── detector.py
    └── go-string-extractor/
        ├── ida-plugin.json      (name: go-string-extractor)
        └── extractor.py
```

HCLI installs the entire suite directory into `$IDAUSR/plugins/<suite-name>/`. Component subdirectories are extracted alongside the root plugin's files. Because `hcli plugin status` only scans one level deep, components are hidden from the top-level listing unless `--show-components` is passed.

Component names must not collide with any installed top-level plugin or with components of other installed suites. HCLI checks for collisions before installing. Uninstalling a component individually is not allowed; uninstall the suite root instead.

Version pins (`==`) and host qualifiers (`@`) are not valid in `components` entries since the components are always bundled in the same archive.

### Plugin suites

Some plugins are distributed as a **suite**: a root plugin that bundles tightly-coupled sub-plugins called components. Components share the suite's lifecycle. They are installed, upgraded, and removed together.

`hcli plugin status` shows a count of components next to each suite. Use `--show-components` to expand the listing:

69	### Plugin identity and name collisions
70	
71	In the repository index, a plugin is identified by the pair `(name, repository URL)`. Two plugins with the same bare name from different repositories are distinct entries, and the repository URL is normalized (lowercased scheme/host/path, trailing slash stripped) before comparison so that cosmetic URL differences do not split a single plugin into two.
72	
73	On disk, however, plugins still install as `$IDAUSR/plugins/<name>`. Name is therefore the installed-layout identity, and only one plugin with a given bare name can be installed at a time. When the repository contains multiple plugins with the same name, HCLI requires a qualified reference of the form `name@repository-url` (optionally with a version spec, e.g. `name==1.2.3@repository-url`). An installed plugin's local metadata records its source repository, so status and upgrade operations anchor their repository lookups on the installed plugin's host and stay consistent even when the bare name is ambiguous in the repository.
